{{Short description|Concept in algebraic geometry}}

In [[algebraic geometry]], a '''morphism of schemes''' generalizes a [[morphism of algebraic varieties]] just as a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] generalizes an [[algebraic variety]]. It is, by definition, a [[morphism]] in the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of schemes.

A [[morphism of algebraic stacks]] generalizes a morphism of schemes.

== Definition ==
By definition, a morphism of schemes is just a morphism of [[locally ringed space]]s. [[Isomorphism]]s are defined accordingly.

A scheme, by definition, has open affine charts and thus a morphism of schemes can also be described in terms of such charts (compare the [[morphism of algebraic varieties#Definition|definition of morphism of varieties]]).<ref>{{harvnb|Vakil|2014|loc=Exercise 6.3.C.}}</ref> Let ƒ:''X''→''Y'' be a morphism of schemes. If ''x'' is a point of ''X'', since ƒ is continuous, there are open affine subsets ''U'' = Spec ''A'' of ''X'' containing ''x'' and ''V'' = Spec ''B'' of ''Y'' such that ƒ(''U'') ⊆ ''V''. Then ƒ: ''U'' → ''V'' is a morphism of [[affine scheme]]s and thus is induced by some [[ring homomorphism]] ''B'' → ''A'' (cf. [[#Affine case]].) In fact, one can use this description to "define" a morphism of schemes; one says that ƒ:''X''→''Y'' is a morphism of schemes if it is locally induced by ring homomorphisms between [[coordinate ring]]s of affine charts.

*'''Note''': It would not be desirable to define a morphism of schemes as a morphism of ringed spaces. One trivial reason is that there is an example of a ringed-space morphism between affine schemes that is not induced by a ring homomorphism (for example,<ref>{{harvnb|Vakil|2014|loc=Exercise 6.2.E.}}</ref> a morphism of ringed spaces:
*:<math>\operatorname{Spec} k(x) \to \operatorname{Spec} k[y]_{(y)} = \{ \eta = (0), s = (y) \}</math>
:that sends the unique point to ''s'' and that comes with <math>k[y]_{(y)} \to k(x), \, y \mapsto x</math>). More conceptually, the definition of a morphism of schemes needs to capture "[[Zariski topology|Zariski-local]] nature" or [[localization of a ring|localization of ring]]s;<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/DAG-V.pdf |title=Derived Algebraic Geometry V: Structured Spaces |date=22 February 2011 |at=§ 1.}}</ref> this point of view (i.e., a local-ringed space) is essential for a generalization ([[topos]]).

Let {{nowrap|''f'' : ''X'' → ''Y''}} be a morphism of schemes with <math>\phi: \mathcal{O}_Y \to f_*\mathcal{O}_X</math>. Then, for each point ''x'' of ''X'', the homomorphism on the stalks:
:<math>\phi: \mathcal{O}_{Y, f(x)} \to \mathcal{O}_{X, x}</math>
is a [[local ring homomorphism]]: i.e., <math>\phi(\mathfrak{m}_{f(x)}) \subseteq \mathfrak{m}_x</math> and so induces an injective homomorphism of [[residue field]]s
:<math>\phi: k(f(x)) \hookrightarrow k(x)</math>.
(In fact, φ maps th ''n''-th power of a maximal ideal to the ''n''-th power of the maximal ideal and thus induces the map between the [[Zariski tangent space|(Zariski) cotangent spaces]].)

For each scheme ''X'', there is a natural morphism

:<math>\theta: X \to \operatorname{Spec} \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X),</math>

which is an isomorphism [[if and only if]] ''X'' is affine; θ is obtained by gluing ''U'' → target which come from restrictions to open affine subsets ''U'' of ''X''. This fact can also be stated as follows: for any scheme ''X'' and a ring ''A'', there is a natural bijection:

:<math>\operatorname{Mor}(X, \operatorname{Spec}(A)) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(A, \Gamma(X, \mathcal O_X)).</math>

(Proof: The map <math>\phi \mapsto \operatorname{Spec}(\phi) \circ \theta</math> from the right to the left is the required bijection. In short, θ is an adjunction.)

Moreover, this fact (adjoint relation) can be used to characterize an [[affine scheme]]: a scheme ''X'' is affine if and only if for each scheme ''S'', the natural map

:<math>\operatorname{Mor}(S, X) \to \operatorname{Hom}(\Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X), \Gamma(S, \mathcal{O}_S))</math>

is bijective.<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1960|loc=Ch. I, Corollarie 1.6.4.}}</ref> (Proof: if the maps are bijective, then <math>\operatorname{Mor}(-, X) \simeq \operatorname{Mor}(-, \operatorname{Spec} \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X))</math> and ''X'' is isomorphic to <math>\operatorname{Spec} \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X)</math> by [[Yoneda's lemma]]; the converse is clear.)
<!--The limit of a (finite) diagram of morphisms of schemes exists;{{fact}} in particular, the fiber product of two morphisms with the same target exists.-->

== A morphism as a relative scheme ==
{{see also|Grothendieck's relative point of view}}
Fix a scheme ''S'', called a '''base scheme'''. Then a morphism <math>p: X \to S</math> is called a scheme over ''S'' or an ''S''-scheme; the idea of the terminology is that it is a scheme ''X'' together with a map to the base scheme ''S''. For example, a [[vector bundle]] ''E'' → ''S'' over a scheme ''S'' is an ''S''-scheme.

An ''S''-morphism from ''p'':''X'' →''S'' to ''q'':''Y'' →''S'' is a morphism ƒ:''X'' →''Y'' of schemes such that ''p'' = ''q'' ∘ ƒ. Given an ''S''-scheme <math>X \to S</math>, viewing ''S'' as an ''S''-scheme over itself via the identity map, an ''S''-morphism <math>S \to X</math> is called a '''''S''-section''' or just a '''section'''.

All the ''S''-schemes form a category: an object in the category is an ''S''-scheme and a morphism in the category an ''S''-morphism. (This category is the [[slice category]] of the category of schemes with the base object ''S''.)

== Affine case ==
Let <math>\varphi: B \to A</math> be a ring homomorphism and let 

:<math>\begin{cases} \varphi^a: \operatorname{Spec} A \to \operatorname{Spec} B, \\ \mathfrak{p} \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{p})\end{cases}</math> 

be the induced map. Then

*<math>\varphi^a</math> is continuous.<ref>Proof: <math>{\varphi^a}^{-1}(D(f)) = D(\varphi(f))</math> for all ''f'' in ''A''.</ref>
*If <math>\varphi</math> is surjective, then <math>\varphi^a</math> is a homeomorphism onto its image.<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1960|loc=Ch. I, Corollaire 1.2.4.}}</ref>
*For every ideal ''I'' of ''A'', <math>\overline{\varphi^a(V(I))} = V(\varphi^{-1}(I)).</math><ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1960|loc=Ch. I, 1.2.2.3.}}</ref>
*<math>\varphi^a</math> has dense image if and only if the kernel of <math>\varphi</math> consists of [[nilpotent]] elements. (Proof: the preceding formula with ''I'' = 0.) In particular, when ''B'' is reduced, <math>\varphi^a</math> has dense image if and only if <math>\varphi</math> is injective.

Let ''f'': Spec ''A'' → Spec ''B''  be a morphism of schemes between affine schemes with the pullback map <math>\varphi</math>: ''B'' → ''A''. That it is a morphism of locally ringed spaces translates to the following statement: if <math>x = \mathfrak{p}_x</math> is a point of Spec ''A'',
:<math>\mathfrak{p}_{f(x)} = \varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{p}_x)</math>.
(Proof: In general, <math>\mathfrak{p}_x</math> consists of ''g'' in ''A'' that has zero image in the [[residue field]] ''k''(''x''); that is, it has the image in the maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}_x</math>. Thus, working in the local rings, <math>g(f(x)) = 0 \Rightarrow \varphi(g) \in \varphi(\mathfrak{m}_{f(x))}) \subseteq \mathfrak{m}_x \Rightarrow g \in \varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m}_x)</math>. If <math>g(f(x)) \ne 0</math>, then <math>g</math> is a unit element and so <math>\varphi(g)</math> is a unit element.)

Hence, each ring homomorphism ''B'' → ''A'' defines a morphism of schemes Spec ''A'' → Spec ''B'' and, conversely, all morphisms between them arise this fashion.

== Examples ==
{{See also|morphism of varieties#Examples}}

=== Basic ones ===
*Let ''R'' be a field or <math>\Z.</math> For each ''R''-algebra ''A'', to specify an element of ''A'', say ''f'' in ''A'', is to give a ''R''-algebra homomorphism <math>R[t] \to A</math> such that <math>t \mapsto f</math>. Thus, <math>A = \operatorname{Hom}_{R-\text{alg}}(R[t], A)</math>. If ''X'' is a scheme over ''S'' = Spec ''R'', then taking <math>A = \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X)</math> and using the fact Spec is a right adjoint to the global section functor, we get <math display="block">\Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X) = \operatorname{Mor}_S(X, \mathbb{A}^1_S)</math> where <math>\mathbb{A}^1_S = \operatorname{Spec}(R[t])</math>. Note the equality is that of rings.
*Similarly, for any ''S''-scheme ''X'', there is the identification of the multiplicative groups: <math display="block">\Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X^*) = \operatorname{Mor}_S(X, \mathbb{G}_m)</math> where <math>\mathbb{G}_m = \operatorname{Spec}(R[t, t^{-1}])</math> is the multiplicative [[group scheme]].
*Many examples of morphisms come from families parameterized by some base space. For example, <math display="block">\text{Proj}\left(\frac{\Complex[x,y][a,b,c]}{(ax^2 +bxy + cy^2)}\right) \to \text{Proj}(\Complex[a,b,c]) = \mathbb{P}^2_{a,b,c}</math> is a projective morphism of projective varieties where the base space parameterizes quadrics in <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>.

=== Graph morphism ===
Given a morphism of schemes <math>f: X \to Y</math> over a scheme ''S'', the morphism <math>X \to X \times_S Y</math> to the [[fiber product of schemes|fiber product]] induced by the identity <math>1_X : X \to X</math> and ''f''  is called the '''graph morphism''' of ''f''. The graph morphism of the identity is called the [[diagonal embedding|diagonal morphism]].

== Types of morphisms ==
{{see also|glossary of algebraic geometry}}

=== Finite type ===
[[morphism of finite type|Morphisms of finite type]] are one of the basic tools for constructing families of varieties. A morphism <math>f:X\to S</math> is of finite type if there exists a cover <math>\operatorname{Spec}(A_i) \to S</math> such that the fibers <math>X \times_S \operatorname{Spec}(A_i)</math> can be covered by finitely many affine schemes <math>\operatorname{Spec}(B_{ij})</math> making the induced ring morphisms <math>A_i \to B_{ij}</math> into [[finitely generated algebra|finite-type morphisms]]. A typical example of a finite-type morphism is a family of schemes. For example,

:<math>\operatorname{Spec}\left(\frac{\Z[x,y,z]}{(x^n + zy^n, z^5-1)} \right) \to \operatorname{Spec}\left(\frac{\Z[z]}{(z^5-1)} \right)</math>

is a morphism of finite type. A simple non-example of a morphism of finite-type is <math>\operatorname{Spec}(k[x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots])) \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)</math> where <math>k</math> is a field. Another is an infinite disjoint union

:<math>\coprod^\infty X \to X</math>

=== Closed immersion ===
A morphism of schemes <math>i:Z \to X</math> is a '''[[closed immersion]]''' if the following conditions hold:
# <math>i</math> defines a homeomorphism of <math>Z</math> onto its image
# <math>i^\#: \mathcal{O}_X \to i_*\mathcal{O}_Z</math> is surjective.
This condition is equivalent to the following: given an affine open <math>\operatorname{Spec}(R) = U \subseteq X</math> there exists an ideal <math>I \subseteq R</math> such that <math>i^{-1}(U) = \operatorname{Spec}(R/I)</math>.

==== Examples ====
Of course, any (graded) quotient <math>R/I</math> defines a subscheme of <math>\operatorname{Spec}(R)</math> (<math>\operatorname{Proj}(R)</math>). Consider the [[Quasi-affine variety|quasi-affine scheme]] <math>\mathbb{A}^2 - \{0 \}</math> and the subset of the <math>x</math>-axis contained in <math>X</math>. Then if we take the open subset <math>\operatorname{Spec}(k[x,y,y^{-1}])</math> the ideal sheaf is <math>(x)</math> while on the affine open <math>\operatorname{Spec}(k[x,y,x^{-1}])</math> there is no ideal since the subset does not intersect this chart.

=== Separated ===
Separated morphisms define families of schemes which are analogous to [[Hausdorff topological space|Hausdorff]] topological spaces. For example, given a separated morphism <math>X \to S</math> in <math>\text{Sch}/\Complex</math> the associated [[analytic space]]s <math>X(\Complex)^{an} \to S(\Complex)^{an}</math> are both Hausdorff. We say a morphism of schemes <math>f:X \to S</math> is separated if the diagonal morphism <math>\Delta_{X/S}:X \to X\times_SX</math> is a closed immersion. In topology, an analogous condition for a space <math>X</math> to be Hausdorff is if the diagonal set

:<math>\Delta = \{(x,x) \in X\times X \}</math>

is a closed subset of <math>X\times X</math>. Nevertheless, most schemes are not Hausdorff as topological spaces, as the Zariski topology is in general highly non-Hausdorff.

==== Examples ====
Most morphisms encountered in scheme theory will be separated. For example, consider the affine scheme

:<math>X = \operatorname{Spec}\left( \frac{\Complex [x,y]}{(f)} \right)</math>

over <math>\operatorname{Spec}(\Complex).</math> Since the product scheme is

:<math>X \times_\Complex X = \operatorname{Spec}\left(\frac{\Complex[x,y]}{(f)}\otimes_\Complex \frac{\Complex[x,y]}{(f)} \right)</math>

the ideal defining the diagonal is generated by<!-- Look in Eisenbud's commutative algebra book, he makes this claim somewhere... -->

:<math>x\otimes 1 - 1 \otimes x, y \otimes 1 - 1 \otimes y</math>

showing the diagonal scheme is affine and closed. This same computation can be used to show that projective schemes are separated as well.

==== Non-examples ====
The only time care must be taken is when [[Gluing schemes|gluing together a family of schemes]]. For example, if we take the diagram of inclusions

:<math>\begin{matrix}
\operatorname{Spec}(R[x,x^{-1}]) & &\\
 &\searrow & \\
&  & \operatorname{Spec}(R[x]) \\
 &\nearrow & \\
\operatorname{Spec}(R[x,x^{-1}]) & &
\end{matrix}</math>

then we get the scheme-theoretic analogue of the classical line with two-origins.

=== Proper ===
A morphism <math>f:X\to S</math> is called [[proper morphism|proper]] if it is
# separated
# of finite type
# universally closed.
The last condition means that given a morphism <math>S' \to S</math> the base change morphism <math>S'\times_SX</math> is a closed immersion. Most known examples of proper morphisms are in fact projective; but, examples of proper varieties which are not projective can be found using [[Toric variety|toric geometry]]. <!-- Cite Fulton's Toric Varieties... -->

=== Projective ===
Projective morphisms define families of [[projective variety|projective varieties]] over a fixed base scheme. Note that there are two definitions: Hartshorne's which states that a morphism <math>f:X\to S</math> is called projective if there exists a closed immersion <math>X \to \mathbb{P}^n_S = \mathbb{P}^n\times S</math> and the [[Éléments de géométrie algébrique|EGA]] definition which states that a scheme <math>X \in \text{Sch}/S</math> is projective if there is a [[quasi-coherent]] <math>\mathcal{O}_S</math>-module of finite type such that there is a closed immersion <math>X \to \mathbb{P}_S(\mathcal{E})</math>. The second definition is useful because an [[exact sequence]] of <math>\mathcal{O}_S</math>-modules can be used to define projective morphisms.

==== Projective morphism over a point ====
A projective morphism <math>f:X \to \{ *\}</math> defines a projective scheme. For example,

:<math>\text{Proj}\left( \frac{\Complex[x,y,z]}{(x^n + y^n - z^n)} \right) \to \operatorname{Spec}(\Complex )</math>

defines a projective curve of genus <math>(n-1)(n-1)/2</math> over <math>\Complex </math>.

==== Family of projective hypersurfaces ====
If we let <math>S = \mathbb{A}^1_t</math> then the projective morphism

:<math>\underline{\operatorname{Proj}}_S\left( \frac{\mathcal{O}_S[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]}{\left(x_0^5 + \cdots + x_4^5 - t x_0 x_1 x_2 x_3 x_4\right)} \right) \to S</math>

defines a family of [[Calabi-Yau manifold]]s which degenerate. <!-- should explain where -->

==== Lefschetz pencil ====
Another useful class of examples of projective morphisms are [[Lefschetz pencil]]s: they are projective morphisms <math>\pi:X \to \mathbb{P}^1_k = \operatorname{Proj}(k[s,t])</math> over some field <math>k</math>. For example, given smooth hypersurfaces <math>X_1, X_2 \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n_k</math> defined by the homogeneous polynomials <math>f_1,f_2</math> there is a projective morphism

:<math>\underline{\operatorname{Proj}}_{\mathbb{P}^1}\left( \frac{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]}{(sf_1 + tf_2)} \right)\to \mathbb{P}^1 </math> 

giving the pencil.

==== EGA projective ====
A nice classical example of a projective scheme is by constructing projective morphisms which factor through rational scrolls. For example, take <math>S = \mathbb{P}^1</math> and the vector bundle <math>\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{O}_S \oplus \mathcal{O}_S \oplus \mathcal{O}_S(3)</math>. This can be used to construct a <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math>-bundle <math>\mathbb{P}_S(\mathcal{E})</math> over <math>S</math>. If we want to construct a projective morphism using this sheaf we can take an exact sequence, such as

:<math>\mathcal{O}_S(-d)\oplus\mathcal{O}_S(-e) \to \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{O}_X \to 0</math>

which defines the structure sheaf of the projective scheme <math>X</math> in <math>\mathbb{P}_S(\mathcal{E}).</math>

=== Flat ===
==== Intuition ====
[[Flat morphism]]s have an algebraic definition but have a very concrete geometric interpretation: flat families correspond to families of varieties which vary "continuously". For example,

:<math>\operatorname{Spec}\left(\frac{\Complex[x,y,t]}{(xy-t))} \right) \to \operatorname{Spec}(\Complex[t])</math>

is a family of smooth affine quadric curves which degenerate to the normal crossing divisor

:<math>\operatorname{Spec}\left(\frac{\Complex[x,y]}{(xy)} \right)</math>

at the origin.

==== Properties ====
One important property that a flat morphism must satisfy is that the dimensions of the fibers should be the same. A simple non-example of a flat morphism then is a blowup since the fibers are either points or copies of some <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math>.

==== Definition ====
Let <math>f:X \to S</math> be a morphism of schemes. We say that <math>f</math> is flat at a point <math>x \in X</math>  if the induced morphism <math>\mathcal{O}_{f(x)} \to \mathcal{O}_x</math> yields an exact functor <math>-\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{f(x)}} \mathcal{O}_x.</math> Then, <math>f</math> is '''flat''' if it is flat at every point of <math>X</math>. It is also '''faithfully flat''' if it is a surjective morphism.

==== Non-example ====
Using our geometric intuition it obvious that

:<math>f:\operatorname{Spec}(\Complex [x,y]/(xy)) \to \operatorname{Spec}(\Complex [x])</math>

is not flat since the fiber over <math>0</math> is <math>\mathbb{A}^1</math> with the rest of the fibers are just a point. But, we can also check this using the definition with local algebra: Consider the ideal <math>\mathfrak{p} = (x) \in \operatorname{Spec}(\Complex [x,y]/(xy)).</math> Since <math>f(\mathfrak{p}) = (x) \in \operatorname{Spec}(\Complex[x])</math> we get a local algebra morphism

:<math>f_{\mathfrak{p}}: \left( \Complex [x] \right)_{(x)} \to \left(\Complex [x,y]/(xy) \right)_{(x)}</math>

If we tensor

:<math>0 \to \Complex[x]_{(x)} \overset{\cdot x}{\longrightarrow} \Complex[x]_{(x)}</math>

with <math>(\Complex[x,y]/(xy))_{(x)}</math>, the map

:<math>(\Complex[x,y]/(xy)))_{(x)} \xrightarrow{\cdot x} (\Complex[x,y]/(xy))_{(x)}</math>

has a non-zero kernel due the vanishing of <math>xy</math>. This shows that the morphism is not flat.

=== Unramified ===
A morphism <math>f:X \to Y</math> of affine schemes is [[unramified morphism|unramified]] if <math>\Omega_{X/Y} = 0</math>. We can use this for the general case of a morphism of schemes <math>f:X\to Y</math>. We say that <math>f</math> is unramified at <math>x\in X</math> if there is an affine open neighborhood <math>x \in U</math> and an affine open <math>V\subseteq Y</math> such that <math>f(U)\subseteq V</math> and <math>\Omega_{U/V} = 0.</math> Then, the morphism is unramified if it is unramified at every point in <math>X</math>.

==== Geometric example ====
One example of a morphism which is flat and generically unramified, except for at a point, is

:<math> \operatorname{Spec}\left( \frac{\Complex [t,x]}{(x^n-t)} \right) \to \operatorname{Spec}(\Complex[t])</math>

We can compute the [[Kähler differential|relative differentials]] using the sequence

:<math>\frac{\Complex[t,x]}{(x^n-t)}\otimes_{\Complex[t]}\Complex[t]dt \to \left(\frac{\Complex[t,x]}{(x^n-t)}dt \oplus \frac{\Complex[t,x]}{(x^n-t)}dx\right) / (nx^{n-1}dx - dt) \to \Omega_{X/Y} \to 0</math>

showing

:<math>\Omega_{X/Y} \cong \left(\frac{\Complex [t,x]}{(x^n-t)}dx\right)/(x^{n-1}dx) \neq 0</math>

if we take the fiber <math>t = 0</math>, then the morphism is ramified since

:<math>\Omega_{X_0/\Complex } = \left(\frac{\Complex[x]}{x^{n}}dx\right)/(x^{n-1}dx)</math>

otherwise we have

:<math>\Omega_{X_\alpha/\Complex} = \left(\frac{\Complex[x]}{(x^n-\alpha)}dx\right)/(x^{n-1}dx) \cong \frac{\Complex[x]}{(\alpha)}dx \cong 0</math>

showing that it is unramified everywhere else.

=== Étale ===
A morphism of schemes <math>f:X \to Y</math> is called '''étale''' if it is flat and unramfied. These are the algebro-geometric analogue of covering spaces. The two main examples to think of are covering spaces and [[finite field extension|finite]] [[separable field extension]]s. Examples in the first case can be constructed by looking at [[Branched covering| branched coverings]] and restricting to the unramified locus.
<!--
Example of a finite surjective unramfied morphism which is not étale https://mathoverflow.net/questions/46176/what-are-unramified-morphisms-like
-->

== Morphisms as points ==
{{see also|rational point#Definition|Functor represented by a scheme}}
By definition, if ''X'', ''S'' are schemes (over some base scheme or ring ''B''), then a morphism from ''S'' to ''X'' (over ''B'') is an ''S''-point of ''X'' and one writes:

:<math>X(S) = \{ f \mid f: S \to X \text{ over } B \}</math>

for the set of all ''S''-points of ''X''. This notion generalizes the notion of solutions to a system of polynomial equations in classical algebraic geometry. Indeed, let ''X'' = Spec(''A'') with <math>A =B[t_1, \dots, t_n]/(f_1, \dots, f_m)</math>. For a ''B''-algebra ''R'', to give an ''R''-point of ''X'' is to give an algebra homomorphism ''A'' →''R'', which in turn amounts to giving a homomorphism

:<math>B[t_1, \dots, t_n] \to R, \, t_i \mapsto r_i</math>

that kills ''f''<sub>''i''</sub>'s. Thus, there is a natural identification:

:<math>X(\operatorname{Spec} R) = \{ (r_1, \dots, r_n) \in R^n | f_1(r_1, \dots, r_n) = \cdots = f_m(r_1, \dots, r_n) = 0 \}.</math>

'''Example''': If ''X'' is an ''S''-scheme with structure map π: ''X'' → ''S'', then an ''S''-point of ''X'' (over ''S'') is the same thing as a section of π.

In [[category theory]], [[Yoneda's lemma]] says that, given a category ''C'',  the contravariant functor
:<math>C \to \mathcal{P}(C) = \operatorname{Fct}(C^{\text{op}}, \mathbf{Sets}), \, X \mapsto \operatorname{Mor}(-, X)</math>
is fully faithful (where <math>\mathcal{P}(C)</math> means the category of [[presheaf (category theory)|presheaves]] on ''C''). Applying the lemma to ''C'' = the category of schemes over ''B'', this says that a scheme over ''B'' is determined by its various points.

It turns out that in fact it is enough to consider ''S''-points with only affine schemes ''S'', precisely because schemes and morphisms between them are obtained by gluing affine schemes and morphisms between them. Because of this, one usually writes ''X''(''R'') = ''X''(Spec ''R'') and view ''X'' as a functor from the category of commutative ''B''-algebras to '''Sets'''.

<!--When a category is embedded into the category of set-valued presheaves on it (Yoneda lemma), finite limits can be computed set-theoretically; thus, one can get for instance:-->
'''Example''': Given ''S''-schemes ''X'', ''Y'' with structure maps ''p'', ''q'',
:<math>(X \times_S Y)(R) = X(R) \times_{S(R)} Y(R) = \{ (x, y) \in X(R) \times Y(R) \mid p(x) = q(y) \}</math>.

'''Example''': With ''B'' still denoting a ring or scheme, for each ''B''-scheme ''X'', there is a natural bijection
:<math>\mathbf{P}^n_B(X) = </math> { the isomorphism classes of line bundles ''L'' on ''X'' together with ''n'' + 1 global sections generating ''L''. };
in fact, the sections ''s''<sub>''i''</sub> of ''L'' define a morphism <math>X \to \mathbf{P}^n_B, \, x \mapsto (s_0(x) : \dots : s_n(x))</math>. (See also [[Proj construction#Global Proj]].)
<!--If ''K'' is an algebraically closed field containing a field ''k'' and ''X'' is a scheme over ''k'', then Spec ''K'' → ''X'' over ''k'' is called a [[geometric point]] of ''X''.-->

'''Remark''': The above point of view (which goes under the name [[functor of points]] and is due to Grothendieck) has had a significant impact on the foundations of algebraic geometry. For example, working with a category-valued [[pseudo-functor|(pseudo-)]]functor instead of a set-valued functor leads to the notion of a [[stack (mathematics)|stack]], which allows one to keep track of morphisms between points (i.e., morphisms between morphisms).

== Rational map ==
{{main|rational map}}

A rational map of schemes is defined in the same way for varieties. Thus, a rational map from a reduced scheme ''X'' to a separated scheme ''Y'' is an [[equivalence class]] of a pair <math>(U, f_U)</math> consisting of an open dense subset ''U'' of ''X'' and a morphism <math>f_U : U \to Y</math>. If ''X'' is irreducible, a [[rational function]] on ''X'' is, by definition, a rational map from ''X'' to the affine line <math>\mathbb{A}^1</math> or the [[projective line]] <math>\mathbb{P}^1.</math>

A rational map is dominant if and only if it sends the generic point to the generic point.<ref>{{harvnb|Vakil|2014|loc=Exercise 6.5.A}}</ref>

A ring homomorphism between function fields need not induce a dominant rational map (even just a rational map).<ref>{{harvnb|Vakil|2014|loc=A paragraph after Exercise 6.5.B}}</ref> For example, Spec ''k''[''x''] and Spec ''k''(''x'') and have the same function field (namely, ''k''(''x'')) but there is no rational map from the former to the latter. However, it is true that any inclusion of function fields of algebraic varieties induces a dominant rational map (see [[morphism of algebraic varieties#Properties]].)
